name: Metoclopramide
summary: Prokinetic that increases lower esophageal sphincter tone and accelerates gastric emptying — first-line for diabetic gastroparesis, with a black-box tardive dyskinesia warning.
mechanism: Dopamine D2 antagonist and 5-HT4 agonist that enhances LES tone, gastric emptying, and small-bowel transit; 5-HT3 antagonism at higher doses adds antiemetic action.

dosing.adult: 10 mg 3–4 times daily, 30 min before meals and at bedtime
dosing.maxDose: 30–40 mg/day; limit continuous use to ≤12 weeks
dosing.renalAdjustment: CrCl < 40 mL/min: reduce dose ~50% and lengthen the dosing interval

safety.pregnancy: Widely used for hyperemesis gravidarum; no major teratogenicity demonstrated
safety.lactation: Excreted in breast milk; considered compatible (may stimulate lactation)
contraindications: History of tardive dyskinesia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome
warnings: Black box: tardive dyskinesia with prolonged/high-dose use — use the lowest dose for the shortest duration (≤12 weeks)
Acute EPS/dystonia, especially children and young adults
monitoring: Involuntary movements — stop at the first sign
safety.overdose: Severe EPS/dystonia — treat dystonia with IV diphenhydramine or benztropine; NMS requires intensive supportive care

clinicalPearls: Acute dystonia (often in young patients, especially women) responds promptly to IV diphenhydramine or benztropine
The TD risk is why guidelines cap use at 12 weeks — reassess rather than refill reflexively
good: First-line prokinetic for gastroparesis and a versatile antiemetic
bad: Continuous use beyond 12 weeks; young patients needing long-term treatment; GI obstruction; Parkinson's disease
